main-inner.text: writing · 日付と時刻 ようび と じこく — days and the clock The seven days, the year–month–day order that runs the opposite of English, and the clock readings that bend the numbers you already know. The seven elemental days Each day is an elemental kanji + 曜日. Sun → Moon → Mars → Mercury → Jupiter → Venus → Saturn — the same planetary order that runs the Romance week, so 火曜日 matches Italian martedì, 金曜日 matches French vendredi. any one of 日 月 火 水 木 金 土 elemental kanji + the marker 曜 · よう + closing 日 日 · び = a day name X 曜日 火曜日 · 水曜日 · 金曜日… The 曜 in the middle is the same character in all seven days — it never changes. The learner's job is just to recognize which elemental kanji goes in the left slot. Once you know the seven elements (日 月 火 水 木 金 土), every day name is one substitution away. 日曜日 にちようび 日 · Sunday 月曜日 げつようび 月 · Monday 火曜日 かようび 火 · Tuesday 水曜日 すいようび 水 · Wednesday 木曜日 もくようび 木 · Thursday 金曜日 きんようび 金 · Friday 土曜日 どようび 土 · Saturday Months are read as numbers of the moon月 · the lunar count 月 · the twelve months — a formula and three exceptions N 月 = N がつ Months are just a number + 月. Plug any 1–12 into the slot and the reading is just that number + がつ. 一月 (いちがつ) · 三月 (さんがつ) · 十月 (じゅうがつ) · 十二月 (じゅうにがつ) Three readings that bend — memorize as exceptions 四月 しがつ April not よんがつ 七月 しちがつ July not なながつ 九月 くがつ September not きゅうがつ Same irregulars as the hours (四 七 九): the on-readings clip into a shorter form. Once these three click, every other month follows the formula. Dates run big to small Year → month → day, biggest unit first, each marked by its kanji (年 / 月 / 日). 年 2024 year · ねん 月 12 month · がつ 日 31 day · にち 二〇二四年十二月三十一日 December 31, 2024 年 ねん Read each digit individually (に・ぜろ・に・よん年) or as a number (にせんにじゅうよねん). 月 がつ Months use the on-readings: 一月 (いちがつ) through 十二月 (じゅうにがつ). 日 にち / か Day-of-month is irregular for 1〜10 + 14, 20, 24 — they take kun-readings ending in か: 一日 ついたち, 二日 ふつか, 三日 みっか, 廿日 はつか. Everything else takes にち. Reading the clock 〜時 for hours, 〜分 for minutes, 半 for half-past — three of the hours bend their reading (四 七 九). 時 · the hours 1 〜 12 1 一時 いちじ 2 二時 にじ 3 三時 さんじ 4 四時 よじ not しじ 5 五時 ごじ 6 六時 ろくじ 7 七時 しちじ not ななじ 8 八時 はちじ 9 九時 くじ not きゅうじ 10 十時 じゅうじ 11 十一時 じゅういちじ 12 十二時 じゅうにじ 分 · the minutes 1 一分 いっぷん pun 2 二分 にふん fun 3 三分 さんぷん pun 5 五分 ごふん fun 10 十分 じゅっぷん pun 30 三十分 さんじゅっぷん 半はん pun fun after 2, 4, 5, 7, 9 — the plain reading. pun after 1, 3, 6, 8, 10 — rendaku-driven, often paired with a small っ in the kana (いっぷん, さんぷん, ろっぷん). 半 (han) replaces "30 minutes" — 三時半 is "three thirty," not "three hours and a half." 午前 · 午後 — AM and PM 午前 ごぜん AM — before noon 午後 ごご PM — after noon AM/PM markers PRECEDE the hour: 午前九時 (ごぜん くじ) is 9 AM, 午後三時半 (ごご さんじはん) is 3:30 PM. The 24-hour clock just keeps counting: 十八時三十分 is 18:30. 時刻 · convert any time to Japanese 十二 三 六 九 時 hour 0–23 分 min 0–59 ⇄ flip AM/PM 日本語で · in Japanese 午前九時三十分 / 午前九時半 ごぜん くじ さんじゅっぷん / ごぜん くじはん 9:30 AM Two ways to set the time. Type the hour (0–23) and minute (0–59) into the inputs, or grab the clock hands and drag — both paths stay in sync. main-inner.text: writing · grammar ぶんの くみたて — building a Japanese sentence If English is a line, Japanese is a constellation. Words can sit almost anywhere — what matters is the little tag that follows each one, and the verb that pins everything to the end. 一 A different way of saying the same thingenglish vs japanese English uses word order to tell you who's doing what to whom. Japanese uses little markers called particles — and the verb almost always lands at the very end. English I watch anime. Word order = meaning. Subject → Verb → Object. Move "I" and "anime" and the sentence breaks. vs. Japanese 私は アニメを 見る。 Particles = meaning. Each noun carries a marker telling its job. The verb sits at the end. So は tags watashi as the topic. を tags anime as the thing being watched. Once those tags are in place, the order can shuffle — and the meaning still holds. 二 The verb is the anchor動詞 / どうし Picture every Japanese sentence as a planet. The verb sits at the center. Everything else orbits — and each piece of information clips on with its own little particle. 読みやすい順 natural order — verb arrives last 田中さん は Topic主題 月曜日 に Time時間 学校 で Location場所 先生 と With同伴者 本 を Object目的語 終わり· the end 読みます Verb動詞 Tanaka-san reads a book with the teacher at school on Monday. 全部の助詞 · all eight particles, by role は Topic 主題 — what we're talking about 田中さんは を Object 目的語 — what the verb acts on 本を に Time 時間 — when it happens 月曜日に に Destination 行き先 — where it's heading 学校に で Location 場所 — where it happens 学校で で Means 手段 — how it's done 電車で から Origin 出発点 — where it starts 駅から と Co-participant 同伴者 — who's along 先生と The verb arrives last. Everything before it is optional — even the topic は. Word order tweaks the emphasis, but rarely the underlying meaning. 三 Four kinds of building blocklike clip-together pieces If we colour every word in a Japanese sentence by its part of speech, only four colours come back. Memorise these four shapes and you'll see the seams in every sentence. 名詞 noun Nouns & な-adjectives The "things" of the sentence: people, places, ideas. な-adjectives feel like nouns and behave like them. 私 · 学校 · アニメ · 静か(な)watashi · gakkou · anime · shizuka 動詞 verb Verbs & い-adjectives Words that conjugate. い-adjectives count here too — they take tense and negation just like verbs. 見る · 食べる · 行く · 寒い · 楽しいmiru · taberu · iku · samui · tanoshii 助詞 Particles & です The tiny clips that label nouns and glue clauses together. です belongs here too — it's grammar, not vocabulary. は · が · を · に · で · の · と · ですwa · ga · o · ni · de · no · to · desu 。 Sentence ender The full stop. In Japanese it's the little circle 。 — and once you reach it, the sentence is sealed. 見る。"watch (period)" Notice the shapes: nouns and verbs are arrows that pass meaning forward. Particles are diamonds that snap between them. The full stop is the cap on the end. 四 Snap the pieces togetheryour first sentence Let's build "I watch anime." Each block clips onto the next — and the diamond particles are what hold the noun arrows in place. "I watch anime." WATASHI WA ANIME WO MITEIRU。 私 watashi は アニメ anime を 見ている miteiru 。 私 (watashi)I — the topic は (wa)topic marker アニメ (anime)the thing watched を (wo)object marker 見ている (miteiru)am watching 五 Now make it longersame shape, more pieces The same clip-together rule scales. Add more nouns, more particles, more clauses — but every new noun still needs its own diamond, and the verb still anchors the end. "I'm a fool who watches anime." WATASHI WA ANIME WO MIRU BAKA DESU。 私 は アニメ を 見る バカ です 。 私I はtopic marker アニメanime (object) をobject marker 見るwatch — modifies バカ バカfool — the predicate ですcopula "am" See what happened? を still says "the thing being watched is anime" — even though the action of watching is now describing a person (バカ), not the speaker directly. Particles stay glued to their noun no matter what's happening around them. "I watch anime with my cute cat." WATASHI WA WATASHI NO KAWAII NEKO TO ANIME WO MIRU。 私 は 私 の 可愛い 猫 と アニメ を 見る 。 私 の 可愛い 猫"my cute cat" — one big noun phrase と (to)co-participant — "with" アニメthe object を (wo)object marker 見るthe verb, anchoring it all 六 Word order changes the spotlightsame sentence, different emphasis Because particles do the labelling, you can shuffle the satellites around the verb. The verb stays at the end — but whatever sits closest to it gets the most weight. NeutralStandard order — no special emphasis. 太郎は 日曜日に 公園で 野球を しました。 Taro played baseball at the park on Sunday. When-focusedTime slid toward the front, then verb. 日曜日に 太郎は 公園で 野球を しました。 On Sunday, Taro played baseball at the park. What-focusedObject hugged up next to the verb. 太郎は 公園で 日曜日に 野球を しました。 It was baseball Taro played at the park on Sunday. Try saying each line out loud — the meaning stays put, but the colour of the sentence shifts. 七 Only two rules are non-negotiableeverything else can move 壱 The verb goes at the end Whatever the sentence is doing — saying, asking, describing — the verb (or です) is the last thing before the full stop. If your sentence is ending in a noun, you're missing your anchor. 弐 Particles follow their noun The diamond always sits immediately after the noun it's tagging. You can move a noun-and-its-particle as a single unit — but you can never separate them. 八 Two pairs that trip everyone upは vs が, に vs で These are the famous confusions. They feel like the same thing at first — but they tell different stories. は vs. が は · topic Sets up what the sentence is about. Old information — already on the table. 私は学生です。As for me — student. が · subject Identifies who or what. New information, often emphatic. 私が学生です。I am the student (not them). に vs. で に · existence / destination Where someone is, or where they're going to. 図書館にいます。I am at the library. で · place of action Where something happens. The action's stage. 図書館で勉強します。I study at the library. You've got the skeleton. Next: walk through each particle individually, and start writing your own sentences from scratch. Study the particles →

main-inner.text: pitch accent · 抑揚 抑揚よくようとトーン How Japanese rises and falls — and why it matters. 一 どうしてピッチが大切？ Why pitch matters Japanese is a mora-timed, pitch-accented language. Unlike English (which uses stress — louder syllables) Japanese uses pitch — higher or lower mora — to mark meaning. Every word has a pitch pattern, and changing it can change the word entirely. The classic example is 橋はし (a bridge), 箸はし (chopsticks), and 端はし (an edge). All three are pronounced hashi. The pitch decides which — tap the speaker on each card to hear it (how clearly they differ depends on your device's Japanese voice). は し が 平板 heiban [0] 端 edge は し が 中高 nakadaka [2] 橋 bridge は し が 頭高 atamadaka [1] 箸 chopsticks 二 よっつのパターン The four patterns Tokyo-standard Japanese has exactly four pitch accent patterns. Once you can hear the four, you can hear every word. The number in brackets [n] tells you how many mora are high before the drop — [0] means no drop (heiban), [1] means drop right after the first mora, etc. 平板 heiban [0] さ く ら が sakura — cherry blossom Heiban (平板) is flat — the pitch rises after the first mora and stays high. The following particle stays high too. Most Japanese nouns are heiban. 頭高 atamadaka [1] は し が hashi [1] — chopsticks Atamadaka (頭高) is head-high — the FIRST mora is high, then drops. The fall comes immediately after mora 1. はし with this pitch means "chopsticks." 中高 nakadaka [2] は し が hashi [2] — bridge Nakadaka (中高) drops somewhere in the middle (or at the end of) the word. はし with the drop AFTER mora 2 means "bridge" — the particle が catches the fall. 尾高 odaka [2] は な が hana — flower Odaka (尾高) looks flat on the word alone — は-な both rise — and only reveals the drop on the NEXT particle: は-な-↓が. The classic pair is 花 (flower, odaka) vs 鼻 (nose, heiban): identical said alone, but 花が falls on が while 鼻が stays high. 三 きごう Notation legend Common marks you'll see across textbooks and dictionaries. This app uses the OJAD-style line above the mora row — high mora sit under the line, low mora outside it. ￣High plateau The OJAD line above kana marks the high-pitch run. Mora under it are H; mora outside it are L. ↓Down-step A vertical drop at the end of a high plateau. The next mora is L, even if visually it sits on the same baseline. ↑Rising tone Question intonation. Add an upward sweep at the END of a sentence to mark it as a question, even without か. ／Pause A small breath between words or phrases. Written as a space in this app; spoken as a brief silence (~100-150ms). ＝Long sustain A held vowel or katakana long mark (ー). The mora is held for two beats but stays at the same pitch. 四 かきかた Notation shortcut You can write pitch accent inline anywhere on this site. Type a kana word followed by a brace of H / L marks — one per mora — and it renders the line over the kana: ありがとう{LHLLL} …turns into: あ り が と う L stands for low, H for high. One mark per mora — small kana fuse to the mora before them (きょ is one), and ー, っ, ん each count on their own. Write the reading in kana (kanji don't split into mora). A few more: に ほ ん ご (heiban), わ た し (nakadaka), あ め (atamadaka), お す し (the sushi word). Ready to practice? 話す Speaking · Shadowing Studio
